topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: The language describes storage duration and object lifetime; the operating system maps virtual address regions with permissions and backing relationships. These views overlap but are not identical. This Linux exercise inspects its own process mappings and prints addresses of representative objects without assuming a fixed order, fixed address, or universal correspondence between a C++ variable and a named executable section.

The language, allocator, virtual-memory manager, and physical-memory accounting describe different things.

blocks.text: HarborWorks needs to investigate memory without turning familiar labels into assumptions. This chapter builds a map of a running process while preserving an important boundary: the C++ standard defines objects and lifetimes, not a universal diagram with the heap always below the stack. Use the diagram as a way to ask questions, then obtain evidence from the actual platform.

topics.title: 3.1.1 Understanding Code and Read-Only Data
topics.summary: Native executable formats commonly separate machine code and read-only data into sections that the loader maps with suitable permissions. Shared libraries add their own mappings, and address-space randomization can change locations between executions. The exact layout depends on the platform, linker options, executable format, and loader behavior.

blocks.text: C++ const qualification is a language access rule, not a promise that every const object occupies a read-only page. A const local object can reside in ordinary stack storage, and optimization can eliminate independent storage. Conversely, attempting to modify read-only mapped memory is a platform protection fault rather than a valid way to test const correctness.

blocks.text: Executable code and read-only data often occupy differently protected mappings in a native process. The executable file contains information the loader uses to establish those mappings, along with metadata for linking and runtime initialization. The resulting process also contains mappings for shared libraries, anonymous memory, stacks, and platform facilities. One source file therefore does not correspond to one contiguous region in the running address space.

blocks.text: The word “text” has a historical meaning in executable inspection: it commonly refers to machine code, not prose. A string literal can be placed in read-only data, but the exact section names and placement are toolchain details. A const declaration expresses a language-level restriction through that interface; it does not, by itself, promise a specific page permission or file section. The example calls its constant a read-only candidate for that reason.

blocks.text: Read a Linux mapping as a range plus properties. The range describes virtual addresses. The permissions indicate allowed page-level operations. A pathname, when present, associates the mapping with a backing object; an anonymous mapping may have no ordinary pathname. These observations help classify regions, but they do not inventory every live C++ object inside them. A writable mapping can hold many objects with independent lifetimes. (PROC)

blocks.text: Distinguish executable sections from loadable segments. Sections organize information for linking and other tools; segments describe groups the loader maps for execution. A debugger, object-file inspector, and /proc reader can therefore display different groupings without disagreeing. Start by asking which representation each tool reports. Do not force a section-oriented explanation onto every runtime mapping.

blocks.text: For the worked program, printing an object’s address is an observation, not an invitation to dereference neighboring bytes. Locate the mapping that contains the address only after validating the range comparison in an external inspection tool or careful parser. The fact that a page is readable does not authorize arbitrary typed reads across unrelated objects. Page protection is coarser than C++ ownership and lifetime, so an apparently accessible address can still be invalid for the operation being attempted.

topics.title: 3.1.2 Understanding Initialized and Uninitialized Data
topics.summary: Static-storage objects have initialization rules, including zero initialization before later applicable initialization stages. Executable formats often represent initialized writable data separately from zero-filled storage commonly associated with BSS. The loader can establish zero-filled memory without storing every zero byte in the executable file.

blocks.text: The phrase uninitialized data section can be misleading at the C++ level: a static int without an explicit initializer is zero-initialized, not an indeterminate local integer. Keep file-format terminology separate from language initialization semantics. Reading an ordinary uninitialized automatic int is not justified by the fact that some executable section is called BSS.

blocks.text: An initialized namespace-scope integer and a zero-initialized namespace-scope integer have different source declarations, but both have defined initial values before the relevant program use. The executable does not necessarily need to store a long sequence of zero bytes for every zero-initialized object. A loader can establish zero-filled storage as part of creating the process. This is why the size of an executable file and the amount of memory its initial image requires are different measurements.

blocks.text: The common .data and .bss labels are useful implementation vocabulary. They are not substitutes for the language’s initialization rules. Constant initialization, zero initialization, and dynamic initialization describe how objects obtain values; section placement describes a particular binary organization. An object requiring runtime construction can involve both reserved storage and initialization code. A section name alone does not prove that an arbitrary global object is ready for use at a particular cross-translation-unit initialization point.

blocks.text: The worked program checks the zero-initialized integer’s value, not its exact address. That is a portable semantic fact about the declaration. It prints addresses to connect those objects to the process map on the Linux lab machine. Treat those two activities differently in a test: one assertion protects a language requirement, while the other supplies observational evidence that can legitimately vary between executions.

blocks.text: Address-space layout randomization and position-independent builds can change where mappings appear. A test that expects a global at a copied numerical address is usually testing an accident of one launch rather than the program’s contract. Even without randomization, a compiler, linker, library, or source change can alter layout. Use relationships supported by the language or inspect current ranges; do not rely on a previously observed address as a persistent identifier.

blocks.text: When investigating startup memory, separate static footprint from later demand. A large zero-filled region can reserve virtual space without every page being resident immediately. Touching pages can change residency. Conversely, a small executable can allocate a large amount at runtime. Record the measurement name, unit, time, and workload phase before comparing two numbers. “Memory increased” is not an actionable observation until you know which memory measure increased and what happened between samples.

topics.title: 3.2.1 Understanding Stack Memory
topics.summary: Many implementations use thread stacks for call frames and some automatic objects, but C++ specifies automatic storage duration rather than one universal physical stack layout. Registers, inlining, tail-call transformations, and optimization can change where or whether an object is materialized. Each thread also has its own execution stack arrangement under the platform runtime.

blocks.text: Automatic storage duration means an object’s lifetime is tied to execution of its block or function according to language rules. A stack is a common implementation mechanism for many such objects, but the compiler may keep values in registers or eliminate independent storage. This distinction prevents the beginner’s shortcut “every local variable is on the stack” from becoming a false rule.

blocks.text: A function call can require storage for saved state, spills, local objects, alignment, and other ABI-defined needs. Recursive calls can create additional active invocations, but the amount of stack consumed per invocation is not simply the sum of the source variables’ sizes. Optimization can inline calls, reuse slots, or transform eligible recursion. Debug builds and instrumented builds can have substantially different stack behavior from release builds.

blocks.text: The lifetime boundary still applies when an address appears unchanged. Returning a pointer or reference to an ordinary local object does not extend that object’s life. The bytes may remain visible for a while, but the program no longer has a valid object to access through that stale reference. A repeated successful read is not evidence that the reference is safe. The object-lifetime rule is the relevant contract. (LIFETIME)

blocks.text: Threads commonly have separate stacks, while sharing much of the process address space. That does not mean a pointer into another thread’s automatic objects is inherently safe or inherently forbidden. Safety depends on lifetime, synchronization, and access rules. Passing a pointer to a local buffer to a worker that outlives the creating scope is a lifetime defect even when the address remains mapped. Joining before destruction can establish the required lifetime relationship for a bounded design.

blocks.text: Do not test stack limits by unbounded recursion in a shared environment. Use a small call chain and inspect its frames with a debugger, then reason about growth separately. The purpose is to understand active invocations, not to crash the host. For algorithms with potentially deep input-dependent recursion, use explicit bounds or an iterative representation when appropriate. A production failure caused by stack exhaustion is not repaired merely by making the stack larger without examining the input and recursion contract.

blocks.text: An allocator may obtain larger blocks from the operating system and satisfy many small allocations from those blocks. Releasing one object can return its storage to the allocator without immediately returning pages to the operating system. Therefore, a stable or elevated resident-memory measurement after deallocation does not by itself prove that the object remains live. Conversely, a stable resident footprint does not prove the absence of logical leaks when freed pages or unused capacity hide growth.

blocks.text: A more useful memory investigation tracks several quantities: live application objects, bytes requested through a particular allocator, container capacity, virtual mappings, and resident pages. Chapter 4 introduces a scoped allocation counter that measures one of those quantities honestly. It does not claim to measure allocator metadata, every library allocation, or physical memory. Naming the quantity prevents a narrow instrument from producing an overly broad conclusion.

blocks.text: Ownership remains the first defense against leaks. A container or RAII wrapper makes the release point explicit and handles ordinary exceptional exits. But RAII alone does not bound how much live data a program retains. A queue whose owner lives forever can grow forever while every allocation is correctly owned. Later chapters add capacity limits and backpressure because lifetime correctness and resource-budget correctness are separate requirements. A system needs both to remain operational under sustained input.

topics.title: Failure clinic — “The address is still there”
topics.summary: A developer returns a pointer to a local buffer and tests it immediately. The expected text appears, so the function is declared correct. The test has observed residual bytes, not a continuing object lifetime. The repair is to return an owned value or arrange an explicit caller-owned buffer whose lifetime covers the use. Repeated execution cannot turn an expired object into a valid one.

Add a dynamically allocated vector with a documented bounded size. Record its data pointer, size, and capacity before and after a deliberate growth operation. Do not dereference the old pointer after a reallocation. The exercise should demonstrate invalidation by comparing the documented operation and current ownership, not by executing an invalid access and hoping for a crash.

Next add a function returning an owned std::string. Compare its lifetime story with a hypothetical function returning a pointer to a local character array. Keep the invalid version as written analysis only; it need not be executed. Identify the owner that survives the return and the point where the owned result is eventually destroyed.

On a Linux development VM, compare a process summary before and after touching a bounded allocated buffer. Explain why virtual size, resident size, and requested allocation size can differ. Do not promise that a particular memory tool will show an exact delta; runtime and allocator behavior contribute to the observation.

Review reasoning. Does a writable mapping contain a valid object of every type? No. Must dynamic storage live in one mapping labeled heap? No. Does const specify an exact executable section? No. Does unchanged residency prove a leak? No. What does an expired local reference violate? The object’s lifetime contract, even if its old page remains accessible.

Completion criterion. Produce a two-column report: semantic obligations on one side, observed implementation details on the other. The ability to keep those categories separate is the foundation for reliable native-memory diagnosis.
